The Town Clerk is the keeper of the public records, and is responsible for all elections, both State and local, held within the community. The Clerk's Office records and issues marriage certificates, issues certified copies of marriage, birth, and death records.

Marriage Intentions

Please click on the sidebar for the application for Marriage. You may fill this out (black ink only) and bring it to the Town Office for completion. DO NOT sign the application! This must be done in front of us. Please bring with you identification (photo identification). If either party has been divorced, we need the original divorce decree (must have the raised seal by the Judge's signature) or if one of you are a widow or widower, we need a copy of the death certificate.

Also, please keep in mind the process takes about a half-hour to complete at the Town Office.

To request a certified copy(s) of a Marriage License, Birth and/or Death Certificate

please click here.

Copies are $15 for the first copy, $6 for each additional at that time.

Please mail the completed form, copy of your identifying documentation, check and a self-addressed stamp envelope to:

Attn: Deputy Clerk, Town of New Gloucester, 385 Intervale Road, New Gloucester, ME 04260

PUBLIC SAFETY MESSAGE

The Fire-Rescue Department is having a difficult time locating addresses for emergency calls they receive because either street numbers are not visible from the roadway or are missing entirely. In addition, SAD 15 school bus drivers, delivery drivers, mail carriers and your friends need to locate your address.

All numbering should be a MINIMUM OF 4 INCHES in height on the dwelling and a MINIMUM OF 4 INCHES in height on a post, fence, wall or mailbox, per Town of New Gloucester Ordinance for Street Naming and Property Numbering Section 6.a.

The department covers approximately 48 square miles that make up the community which has seen substantial growth over the past several years while still maintaining some rural character. Well trained and dedicated “on-call” personnel and a fulltime fire chief respond to all types of emergencies including fires, medical calls, accidents, hazardous materials, and off-road incidents - to name a few.

The department has eight response vehicles including two engines, two tankers, a squad truck, a pickup truck, and an ambulance. The department still has in running condition its first fire engine, a 1928 Model-A engine.

The department handles on average 550 calls each year. Our staff is active and well trained putting in over 2500 hours annually in training and over 10,000 hours responding to calls. The department actively participates with its neighbouring departments in mutual aid emergency responses and trainings.

To see more of what’s happening in the department follow us on facebook: http://www.facebook.com/newgloucesterfirerescue

title: Historical Society
heading: New Gloucester Historical Society
html:
This summer is going by so fast and the New Gloucester Historical Society has been keeping very busy: Avis Ford and her helpers provided the treats for Town Meeting in May, Kathie Anderson and her many volunteers had a very successful Strawberry Festival in June, and on July 4th the Society had the annual reading of the Declaration of Independence, with several people attending.

President Beverly Cadigan, Diantha Grant, and Tom Blake spent many hours getting the History Barn ready for the opening of our new special exhibit, “THE FARM” ~ The Opportunity Farm 1910 – 2011.

For the debut on June 7th, the doors of the History Barn opened to many visitors between 9:00 AM and noon with about 100 people attending. Many of them were past residents of the Opportunity Farm, spending time looking at the photo albums, videos and even enjoying coffee and fresh Thompson’s Orchards donuts, and a good time was had by all that attended the opening. DON’T MISS THIS REMARKABLE SPECIAL EXHIBIT OF WHAT WAS A VERY IMPORTANT PART OF NEW GLOUCESTER’S HISTORY.

The Society has copies of New Gloucester – Images of America by New Gloucester Historical Society curator Tom Blake, 2025 Historical Society Calendars, and still has some of the limited edition 2024 New Gloucester 250 celebration commemorative coins, all of which can be purchased at the History Barn. Meetings of the Historical Society are open to the public and are held on the third Thursday of the month at the New Gloucester Meeting house on Intervale Road (next to the Town Hall) at 7:00 P.M., and will resume in September.

If you are interested in the history of New Gloucester, please consider becoming a member of the New Gloucester Historical Society to assist with projects and to help gather and preserve New Gloucester history.

The History Barn and Meetinghouse Archives are open the 1st Saturday of each month from 9:00 AM to noon. Please stop by and see the wonderful collection of the New Gloucester Historical Society and join us for our up-coming annual events:

  • Avis’s Apple Pie Sale
  • The Lighting of the Lower Village Christmas Tree “Tiny Timber”

Please click here for the New Gloucester Historical Society Membership Form.

History Information

The New Gloucester Historical Society maintains an archive of books, biographical and genealogical information, manuscripts, journals, and photographs pertaining to the history of New Gloucester, its residents, government, organizations, and architecture. In addition, the Historical Society owns and maintains the History Barn, which is open the 1st Saturday each month from 9:00 A.M. to noon, where they display many artifacts relating to New Gloucester's past, and owns and maintains the Blockhouse site at 70 Gloucester Hill Road.

If you have questions about New Gloucester history or genealogy, or items to donate to the collections, please contact our Librarian/Archivist Linda Gard at linda.gard30@gmail.com or Curator Tom Blake at tsiblake@yahoo.com.

If you would like to receive quarterly email updates and occasional special notices, please email Beverly Cadigan at bjtc4ngmhs@gmail.com.

The New Gloucester Historical Society is a 501(c)3 organization and donations are tax deductible. If you would like to donate, please make checks payable to the New Gloucester Maine Historical Society and mail it to the New Gloucester Historical Society at PO Box 531, New Gloucester, Maine 04260.

New Gloucester Book Signing

Tom Blake will be at the New Gloucester Historical Barn the first Saturday of each month from 9:00 am - 12:00 pm to sell and sign copies of the New Gloucester Historical Society book.

Description:

Define scenic resources, including points (historic buildings), linear resources (scenic roads), and areas (village centers) with public access.

Systematically identify, visit, photograph, and map notable scenic resources—landscapes, view sheds, and landmarks—as seen from key public locations.

Establish a clear, objective baseline of New Gloucester’s scenic character to inform future land use planning, preservation, and community decisions.

title: Charter Commission
heading: Charter Commission
html:
The Charter Commission is made up of the following: Six (6) Elected Members and Three (3) Members appointed by the Board of Selectmen. A Municipal Charter is the basic document that defines the organizations, powers functions and essential procedures of the Town.

  • On August 24, 2022, the Charter Commission sent their Final Report Submission to the New Gloucester Select Board.
  • On Monday, August 29, 2022, the Municipal Officers voted to send the Charter Commission Final Report to the voters at the November 8th, 2022, Election.
  • New Gloucester Charter Adopted November 8, 2022

Below are the final documents:
Copies of these documents will be available at Town Hall

  • Charter Commission Final Report Submission to the Municipal Officers
  • Legal opinion from the Charter Commission Attorney
  • New Gloucester Charter Final Report August 24, 2022

If you would like to be added to the Charter Commission listserv, please send a message to: ngchartercommission@gmail.com

What is a charter?
A charter is the equivalent of a constitution for the town. The charter defines the governance structure of the town, distribution of powers, budget process, public access, and other government functions.

What is the Charter Commission’s charge?
The Charter Commission will draft a charter to submit to the voters of New Gloucester, who will determine whether the town adopts the Charter.

What is New Gloucester’s current governance structure?
New Gloucester’s current governance structure is a Town Meeting-Selectmen-Manager form of government, where town meeting serves as the legislative arm of government, the selectmen serve as the executive body, and the manager oversees the daily operations of the town.

What are the typical governance structures in Maine?

  • Town Meeting-Selectmen
  • Town Meeting-Selectmen-Manager
  • Council-Town Meeting (often for special purposes only, such as budget adoption)-Manager
  • Council-Manager
  • Council-Mayor-Administrator

Comments about the charter process are also welcome at ngchartercommission@gmail.com. All correspondence to and from this email address is a matter of public record.

The recommendations are arrived at by reviewing requests that are being considered by the Town Manager and Select Board. The Committee reviews all capital expenditure requests in the form and funding methods submitted. The New Gloucester Economic and Community Development Committee works to support local businesses, enhance business conditions, and develop community engagement, through actions to:

  1. Develop municipal initiatives that support local businesses and attract new businesses that are compatible with the community, meet the needs of residents, and provide new community revenues.
  2. Leverage the community’s location, setting and character to enhance economic development.
  3. Promote an age-friendly community that is a healthy, active and safe place to live, work, play and age.
  4. Identify community development grants and resources.
  5. Collaborate with town departments and committees, businesses, local volunteer groups, and community service organizations to encourage age-friendly initiatives.

The committee is comprised of seven at-large members, one Select Board Liaison (non-voting) and a staff member.

If you have ever been interested in working to support the business community, and the goals of the committee's mission statement above resonate, please join us. Mission Statement:

It is the mission of the Land Management Planning Committee to assist in the improvement and development of municipal policies affecting growth and conservation in New Gloucester by reviewing ordinances and organizing community planning. In general, the Land Management Planning Committee serves as an advisory board that reviews ordinances and regulations, but the committee has also been asked to develop long range growth management strategies to submit to the town for approval. The committee will be comprised of nine at-large members, Planning Board Representative (non-voting) one Select Board Liaison (non-voting) and a staff member.

Committee Involvement:

In general, the Land Management Planning Committee serves as an advisory board that reviews ordinances and regulations, but the committee has also been asked to develop long range growth management strategies to submit to the town for approval. Current projects include but are not exclusive to: developing an Upper Village master plan, monitoring a hydro-geologic study to determine a potential town water source, and long term road planning.

Meetings:

The Land Management Planning Committee meets regularly on the 4th Wednesday of every month in the New Gloucester Meeting House located at 389 Intervale Road, unless otherwise noted. Committee meetings are open to the public - we encourage you to attend and share your thoughts with us.

The plan was accepted by the State of Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry for January 6,2022 .The plan can be found here. Hardcopy is available in New Gloucester Town Hall. Please contact the Town Planner, if you have additional questions.

Upper Village Master Planning

At a special Town Meeting in 2015, voters supported both a resolution endorsing the Town's ongoing Upper Village Master Planning effort and zoning refinements for the area aimed at fostering village-oriented development there. Since that time, the Land Management Planning Committee has developed a series of voluntary design guidelines for the Upper Village (see sidebar to right), which have been endorsed by the Planning Board as a working draft. The master planning effort for the Upper Village will continue to evolve as the town makes decisions regarding the construction of a new public works facility and seeks to form private/public partnerships for redevelopment in the area.

title: Veterans Monument
heading: New Gloucester Veterans Monument
html:
Veterans Monument

We are announcing that the New Gloucester Veterans Monument has now changed from a committee structure to a non-profit 501(c) (3) corporation.

The purpose is still same: to honor veterans with ties to New Gloucester, including past, present, and future veterans of all branches of the military.

All names of eligible veterans will be added to the Monument at no cost to the veteran. Names are added once a year; the name application form with a copy of a DD-214 or other evidence of having served honorably in the US military, must be received on or before the last day of February each year.

MAPLE TREE REPLACEMENT

In 2017, the New Gloucester Veterans Monument had five maple trees planted behind the monument. Some of you may have noticed four of the trees are growing into beautiful, mature trees, but one is dying and needs to be replaced. The Board is working on the replacement of this tree. The replacement tree should be as near as possible to the same size as the other four trees. The estimated cost of the project is approximately $1,000.

CLEANING THE MONUMENT

The New Gloucester Veterans Monument was constructed more than 10 years ago, and now the bricks and monuments are starting to show signs of soot and grime accumulation brought on by dust, air pollution, and vehicle exhaust.

The New Gloucester Veterans Monument is a place of reflection, gratitude, and respect. It is important that we keep the monument clean and beautiful. We are committed to the highest standards of preservation so we would like to have it professionally cleaned! Anyone interested in contributing to these projects can find a donation form on the sidebar of this webpage.

Forms for adding a veteran’s name or making a donation to the Monument are available on the sidebar on this webpage or email: ngvm.jean2014@gmail.com.

Trustee Statement
During the 1950’s the State and later the Town unknowingly piled road salt on the ground. The result was a slow leaching of salt and chloride into ground water beneath the Upper Village area.

Later, during the 1980’s and early 1990’s, leaking petroleum storage tanks were identified in the Upper Village. While with assistance from Maine DEP the source of contamination was addressed, ground water in the Upper Village was contaminated with petroleum product.

Ground water in much of the Upper Village remains contaminated and cannot be removed. The impacts of the contamination include:

  • considerable health risk to residents
  • a decrease in property values and difficulty financing property sales
  • limitations on the Town’s ability to develop the area for commercial purposes
  • a substantial cost over time to the Town, residents, and business owners

There is one and only one solution to this public health threat and regrettable loss of property value, which will also provide the conditions for future growth – to supply the area with quality water from a protected source.

To that end the State Legislature and District Voters have authorized the creation of the New Gloucester Water District.

The Water District Board of Trustees, in conjunction with Local, State and Federal authorities, are working to design and fund a water system that permanently solves the water quality issues and provides fire protection, reducing insurance costs and encouraging commercial development. When completed in early 2014, the project is expected to increase property values, decrease insurance costs and ensure every person’s right to clean, pure, healthy drinking water.
